name: ldpl
desc: COBOL-like programming language that compiles to C++
why: A COBOL-style language that compiles to C++, an unusual language worth an evening of curiosity.

brief.what_it_is: LDPL is a general-purpose compiled programming language with plain-English, COBOL-inspired syntax. You write source in a .ldpl file using keywords like DISPLAY, ACCEPT, FOR ... DO ... REPEAT and PRINT, and the compiler translates it into C++ and builds a native executable. The README's example prints a greeting in Chinese ten times in a loop. Input is LDPL source text and output is a compiled binary, which by default is named source-bin for a file called source.ldpl. The language supports UTF-8 natively, arbitrarily large integer arithmetic, and interfacing with C and C++ code and libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says LDPL is meant to be easy to understand, learn, write, and use, and that the compiler should handle hard low-level details such as encoding, sockets, and floating-point comparison so the user doesn't have to. The homepage says it was designed to be excessively expressive, readable, fast, and easy to learn, mimicking the good parts of older languages like COBOL.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler translates LDPL code into C++ and then uses a C++ compiler to produce the executable, so a working c++ on the PATH is required. The README says the compiler needs only a single flagless command to build any source. The homepage says LDPL is now in minimal evolution mode, meaning the specification is kept as unchanged as possible.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew and Snap packages are offered, but the README's preferred route is to clone the GitHub repository and run make then make install. It requires only C++11 to compile and run, and works out of the box on Unix systems such as Linux and macOS. The machine needs a C++ compiler reachable as c++ in the PATH, since LDPL emits C++ and relies on it. No accounts, runtimes, or configuration steps were mentioned beyond that.
brief.standout: A COBOL-flavoured, English-like language that is compiled to native code via C++ rather than interpreted, with native UTF-8 and arbitrary-precision integers. Its design rule that every statement does exactly one thing regardless of context, plus a one-command compile with no flags, is a deliberate and unusual stance.
brief.status: Mixed signals. The homepage says the latest release is LDPL 5 Groovy Gualicho from March 27, 2023 and that the language is now in minimal evolution mode. The GitHub README shows a last-release badge of 5.1.0 'Groovy Gualicho', says 5.2 is the current development version and is stable, and carries a note last updated July 4th, 2026, admitting the repository still needs tidying. I could not see commit dates or release dates on the repo page, so I'd call it active but with a stale-looking website.
brief.caveats: The README warns that version 5.1 has a number of known issues and that users should build 5.2 where possible. The README also says the example and documentation pages may be out of date and some examples may need changes for the current version. A C++ compiler is required at runtime, which makes it unlike a standalone interpreter. The README says the examples will be linked soon, and there is a note that its tidying work (updating README files and the website) is still in progress. The README describes the Unix install path only; Windows is not mentioned.
